opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as roughly three or four waves, and each one was a reaction to the limits of the one before.

The first wave was really the classical, model-based era. People came from control theory and mechanical engineering, and the belief was: if you can write down the physics precisely enough — the kinematics, the dynamics, the contact models — then you can plan and control your way to good behavior. And honestly, that wave produced a lot of things that still work beautifully. Industrial arms, the early legged robots, a lot of the locomotion work you see today still has that DNA. But the weakness was that the world is messy. The moment you leave a structured factory cell and face deformable objects, unknown geometry, friction you can't measure, the hand-built models just break down.

The second wave was learning, and it came in a couple of flavors. One was reinforcement learning, especially in simulation — the idea that you don't have to model everything by hand, you let the robot discover behavior through trial and error, then transfer it to the real world. Sim-to-real for locomotion was a huge success story there. The other flavor was imitation learning: instead of rewards, you show the robot what to do. For a while these felt like competing philosophies, but they were both saying the same thing at a deeper level — the behavior should come from data, not from equations a human wrote.

Then the third wave, which we're still in, was shaped by what happened in language and vision. Large models showed that scale and broad pretraining give you generalization you could never hand-engineer. So robotics people asked: can we have a foundation model for robots? That's where vision-language-action models, cross-embodiment datasets, and this whole push toward generalist policies came from. The central question shifted from "what algorithm" to "what data, and how much of it."

And what I find interesting is that data is now the bottleneck in a way it isn't for language. There's no internet of robot actions. So a lot of the energy right now — and this is close to what I care about — is about how you collect data efficiently: better teleoperation, low-cost hardware, human video, simulation again but in a new role. In a sense, the waves loop back. Simulation and modeling come back, not as the controller itself, but as a data engine.

So my summary would be that each wave didn't erase the previous one. It changed where the knowledge lives — first in the engineer's equations, then in the reward or the demonstrations, and now in the data and the model's weights. And the next wave will probably be about closing the loop: robots that are deployed, collect their own experience, and keep improving. That's the part I think nobody has fully cracked yet.

r001.rationale: The response presents successive waves as changing approaches to producing capable robot behavior, and summarizes the shift as knowledge moving from engineers’ equations to rewards or demonstrations, then to data and model weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about the history of robotics, I don't see a straight line so much as a series of pendulum swings, and each swing is really a bet about where intelligence should come from.

The first wave was what people call classical robotics. The core idea was that you could make the world legible through engineering. You model the robot's kinematics precisely, you model the environment, you build a planner on top, and you execute. That gave us industrial arms that are astonishingly reliable inside a cage, where everything is fixed and known. The limitation is obvious in hindsight: the moment the world stops cooperating with your model, the system falls apart. The intelligence lived entirely in the engineer's head.

The second wave was the behavior-based reaction to that, Rodney Brooks and the subsumption architecture. The claim was almost philosophical: the world is its own best model, so stop trying to represent it and instead stack simple reactive behaviors. It produced robots that were robust in a way the classical ones weren't, but it never scaled to complex tasks. You couldn't compose your way to something that could set a table.

Then came the probabilistic era, roughly the late nineties through the DARPA challenges. Sebastian Thrun, SLAM, Bayesian filtering. The insight there was to admit uncertainty into the model instead of pretending it away. That's what got cars across the desert. But perception and control were still largely separate, hand-designed pipelines, and the learning was mostly about state estimation rather than about behavior.

The fourth wave is the deep learning wave, and I'd break it into two phases. First, around 2015 to 2019, deep reinforcement learning, Sergey Levine's work, the idea that you could learn perception and control end to end from pixels. It was exciting but brittle and data hungry, and a lot of it only worked in simulation. Then the second phase, which we're in now, is the foundation model wave. The bet shifted again: instead of learning from scratch per task, you inherit knowledge from internet-scale vision and language, and you collect large, diverse robot datasets so that the policy can generalize. RT-2, the open cross-embodiment efforts, the vision-language-action models. The intelligence now comes from data and scale rather than from the engineer's model or from a reward function.

What I find interesting is that each wave didn't really kill the previous one. The classical control stack is still in every real robot at the lowest level. Probabilistic estimation is still there. What changes is where you draw the boundary of what's learned versus what's designed, and that boundary keeps moving upward as data gets cheaper.

If I had to name the open question for the current wave, it's whether robotics has a true scaling law or whether the physical world is stubborn in a way that text wasn't. Language had the internet sitting there. Robots have to generate their own data by acting, and that's expensive and slow. So the next swing might be about data engines, simulation, and how you get the equivalent of a trillion tokens of embodied experience. That's the thing I'd watch.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the successive waves as changing bets about where robotic intelligence should come from, while describing each wave’s approach to building capable robots.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as successive changes in what researchers believe is the hardest part of robotics. Is it reasoning about what to do? Is it sensing the world accurately? Is it controlling movement? Or is it learning from experience?

Each answer leads to a different wave of ideas. If you emphasize reasoning, you build explicit representations and planners. If you emphasize interaction with the environment, perception, feedback, and behavior become central. If you emphasize learning, you ask how much of that system can be acquired from data rather than designed by hand.

But I wouldn’t describe this as one wave simply replacing another. A robot still needs to act under physical constraints, deal with uncertainty, and recover when something goes wrong. New approaches change how we address those problems; they don’t make the problems disappear.

So the interesting question for me is what each wave makes possible—and which limitations become visible once we actually put those ideas into a robot.

r001.rationale: The response describes successive waves as changing views of robotics’ hardest problems and how to address them. It says those problems persist, but does not frame the waves as different ideas for realizing an enduring aspiration for robotics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as successive shifts in what we believe is the hardest part of intelligence. One wave emphasizes reasoning: if we can represent the world and plan correctly, the robot can act intelligently. Another emphasizes the interaction between perception, action, and the environment: intelligence emerges through doing, not just through thinking. Then learning becomes central—rather than specifying every rule, we let the system acquire capabilities from data and experience.

These ideas don’t simply replace one another. Robotics keeps bringing us back to the same practical question: can the machine actually do the task in the physical world? A strong learning system still needs to deal with control, uncertainty, and safety. A beautifully designed planner still needs reliable perception.

So I would look at each wave by asking what bottleneck it removes, and what it leaves unresolved. The excitement is useful, because it brings people and resources into the field. But the lasting progress comes when those ideas become reliable capabilities, and when we understand how to combine them.

r001.rationale: The response describes successive waves as different approaches—reasoning, perception-action interaction, and learning—and ties them to the enduring practical aspiration of enabling machines to perform tasks in the physical world.
